introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les questions 1 à 12 réparties en quatre sections de trois questions) : filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation ni statistique précise n'est avancée ; les dates, noms, traités et lieux sont ceux de l'historiographie établie, cités de mémoire historique et à faire relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 1 : faits cités de mémoire historique (loi britannique de 1807, escadre navale de 1808, Freetown, Liberia à partir de 1822, traité de Lagos 1851 et annexion 1861, Jaja d'Opobo, expéditions du Niger de 1841, traités antiesclavagistes avec des chefs duala dans les années 1840) ; les dates sont données de façon prudente et aucun chiffre de déportés n'est avancé.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Evaluate the significance of the abolition of slave trade along the coast of West Africa during the 19th century.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The slave trade across the Atlantic had been the main link between West Africa and Europe for over three centuries. Britain made the trade illegal for its subjects by the Act of 1807, set up a naval squadron on the West African coast soon afterwards, and then pressed other powers to follow. To "evaluate the significance" of abolition is to weigh how much it changed West Africa, economically, socially and politically, and to judge whether those changes were deep or only on the surface. It will be argued here that abolition was highly significant, but that its results were mixed: it opened the way to new trade, new communities and new ideas, but it also strengthened slavery inside Africa and prepared European intervention.

**1. Economic significance.**
- *Rise of "legitimate commerce".* Africans now had to find new exports. Palm oil (from the Niger Delta and the Bights of Benin and Biafra), groundnuts (Senegambia), timber, and later cotton and rubber took the place of captives. Palm oil was in great demand in Europe for soap, candles and as a lubricant for machines, so the new trade brought wealth to coastal chiefs and merchants.
- *New trading states and ports.* Rulers who adapted prospered: the "oil rivers" city-states of the Niger Delta, and Jaja of Opobo, who built a powerful palm-oil state from 1870. Dahomey moved increasingly towards palm oil under its kings, although it clung to the slave trade for longer. Lagos and Freetown grew as trading ports.
- *Limits and costs.* Not every region gained. States that had depended on selling captives lost income and some declined. European firms controlled shipping and credit and could fix prices, so West Africa became a supplier of raw materials and a market for imported goods. The change was therefore real but it created a new kind of dependence.

**2. Social significance.**
- *Resettlement of freed Africans.* Africans freed from captured ships were landed at Freetown in Sierra Leone, where a settlement for freed people had been founded in the late 1780s. Freed Americans were settled in Liberia from the 1820s, and the republic declared its independence in 1847. The Krio of Freetown became an educated community which supplied clerks, teachers, clergy and traders to the whole coast.
- *Missionaries and western education.* Anti-slavery was linked with the idea of "Christianity, commerce and civilisation". Missionary societies opened churches and schools, for example at Freetown, Abeokuta and Calabar, and Baptist missionaries from the 1840s on the Cameroon coast. New elites were created who later led nationalist movements.
- *Domestic slavery increased.* Captives who could no longer be sold overseas were kept and used inside Africa to produce and carry palm oil and food. In many societies slavery grew, and this was one of the bitter results of abolition.

**3. Political significance.**
- *Change within African states.* Some old states declined, and the end of the trade in captives was one of the factors in the troubles of states such as Oyo in the early nineteenth century. New powers rose through the new trade. Chiefs on the Cameroon coast, including the Duala, signed anti-slave-trade treaties with British officers in the 1840s and began to deal with consuls who settled their trade disputes.
- *Growing European involvement.* To enforce abolition, Britain used treaties, naval patrols and, when necessary, force. Lagos was bombarded in 1851 to remove a ruler who favoured the trade and was annexed in 1861. The Niger expeditions, such as that of 1841, tried to replace the trade by "Christianity and commerce". Anti-slavery thus became a reason to interfere in African affairs, and the need to protect trade and missions led the powers, from the 1870s and 1880s, to claim the coast and then the interior. In the long run abolition helped to open the way to colonial rule.

**4. Evaluation.** The abolition of the slave trade was a turning point: it ended a cruel trade which had depopulated and disturbed many societies, it created new exports, new educated communities and new links with Christianity and Western education. But its significance should not be exaggerated as a purely humane act. The trade went on illegally for decades because of continuing demand in the Americas, slavery inside Africa expanded, and the policy of enforcement finally served European economic and political interests.

**Conclusion.** The abolition of the slave trade was significant above all because it changed the basis of West Africa's relations with the outside world, from the export of people to the export of produce, and because it brought missionaries, consuls and gunboats to the coast. Its effects were therefore both constructive and dangerous, and its fullest consequences, the European partition of the continent, appeared only after 1880.
